evidence.title: A Novel Playbook for Pragmatic Trial Operations to Monitor and Evaluate Ambient Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: ICD-10 accuracy after template redesign and targeted user training
evidence.effect: Accuracy fell from 79% to 35% after template change and returned to baseline after note template redesign and user training
evidence.quote: A brief workflow issue related to a note template change initially reduced ICD-10 documentation accuracy from 79% (95% confidence interval [CI], 72 to 86%) to 35% (95% CI, 28 to 42%); accuracy returned to baseline after note template redesign and user training.

evidence.title: Targeted Interventions Lead to Quality Improvement in Year 2 of an Artificial Intelligence-Based Diabetic Retinopathy Detection Program in Northern California
evidence.effect: The AI system's gradability increased from 62.3% in Year 1 to 71.2% in Year 2 following targeted training.
evidence.quote: The AI system's gradability increased from 62.3% in Year 1 to 71.2% in Year 2, comparable to non-mydriatic gradability rates observed in clinical trials.

evidence.title: Academic Detailing to Enhance Adoption of Clinical Decision Support for Patients at Risk of Opioid Overdose
evidence.outcome: Prescription-to-alert ratio after targeted emails to 150 low-responding providers
evidence.effect: Ratio rose from 9.3% to 50.6%, a 41.3% absolute increase (95% CI 36.9-45.7%, p<0.001), sustained for 8 months.
evidence.quote: The second intervention resulted in an increased prescription-to-alert ratio from 9.3 to 50.6%, an absolute increase of 41.3% when comparing the nearly 8 months before and after the emails were sent (95% CI: 36.9-45.7%, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Improving Nurses' Management of Uterine Tachysystole
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
evidence.effect: Timely management with evidence-based intervention significantly improved after targeted retraining via an educational intervention (p < .001).
evidence.quote: Phase II found a significant improvement in the timely management of tachysystole with evidence-based intervention in the presence of Category II/III fetal heart rate pattern ( p < .001).

commentary.bottom_line: Four real-deployment studies report that targeted retraining after monitoring detected misuse or low uptake was followed by recovered or improved performance, including a rise in prescription-to-alert ratio from 9.3% to 50.6%. None of the studies used a concurrent comparison group, so the gains may partly reflect other changes made at the same time.

perspectives.view: One quasi-experimental study and three uncontrolled before-after studies all point in the same direction. The designs start at low certainty and carry serious risk of bias, and the tools and outcomes differ across studies. The 41.3% absolute increase (95% CI 36.9-45.7%) is precise, but it comes from a single uncontrolled study, which leaves certainty very low.

In one site, ICD-10 accuracy fell from 79% to 35% after a template change and returned to baseline after redesign and user training. This suggests that monitoring can detect a degradation and that a combined response can reverse it. Because training was paired with redesign, the study cannot show how much of the recovery came from retraining alone.

Targeted emails to 150 low-responding providers were followed by a gain that lasted 8 months. AI image gradability rose from 62.3% to 71.2% after targeted training. These results suggest that low-intensity interventions aimed at identified users can fit into existing workflows. None of the studies reported the staff time or fidelity of delivery.

The interventions described were modest in scale, with an email campaign to 150 providers and an education module completed by 66 nurses. This suggests that retraining focused on the users that monitoring flags may cost less than retraining everyone. None of the studies reported cost or staffing figures.

After retraining, labor nurses managed tachysystole with evidence-based interventions in a more timely way (p < .001). That outcome relates directly to care for mothers and infants. The study did not report patient-reported experience or clinical outcomes beyond nursing actions.

None of the four studies reported the payer mix, safety-net status, language, or literacy of the patients served. Two studies did not report their country. The evidence therefore cannot show whether retraining corrects misuse that falls unevenly on underserved patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared targeted retraining against a concurrent control or separated the effect of training from tool or template changes made at the same time. None measured patient outcomes, cost, or staff burden. No study tested whether lessons from AI retirement reviews or vendor exits carry into future training, even though one endorsing framework calls for this.
commentary.underserved_note: No study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the effect of retraining in those settings is unknown and should be monitored locally.
